value.overview: The Speckled Mourner (Laniocera rufescens) is a quiet, inconspicuous forest bird of the tityra and becard family, Tityridae. It has mainly warm brown plumage, subtle spotting or scalloping on the breast, and a thin orange eye-ring. This species usually remains in dense tropical forest, where it searches foliage and branches for food. It is rarely seen compared with many other lowland forest birds, partly because it often perches silently and moves unobtrusively through shaded vegetation.
value.classification: The Speckled Mourner belongs to the family Tityridae and the genus Laniocera. It is one of two living species of Laniocera, the other being the Cinereous Mourner of South America.
value.identification: This medium-sized mourner is mostly rufous-brown above, with a paler cinnamon-brown throat and underparts. The breast commonly shows fine dusky scalloping, while the wing coverts have rufous spots that may form two faint wing-bars. Adults have a narrow orange eye-ring, a dark bill with a paler lower-bill base, and brownish-gray legs. The sexes are similar, although males may have concealed pale yellow or orange pectoral tufts. It can resemble the plainer, heavier-billed Rufous Piha.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southeastern Mexico through much of Central America to northwestern Colombia, with additional populations in western Colombia and northwestern Ecuador. In Costa Rica it occurs on both Caribbean and Pacific slopes, including central and southern Puntarenas, but is generally considered uncommon or rare. It inhabits humid evergreen lowland forest, especially wetter places near streams, swamps, and other damp forest habitats. Most records are from sea level to about 800 meters in Costa Rica.
value.migrationStatus: The Speckled Mourner is considered a year-round resident. In Costa Rica, it is present throughout the year rather than being a regular seasonal migrant, although local movements may occur in response to food and habitat conditions.
value.breeding: The breeding biology of the Speckled Mourner remains poorly documented. Available observations indicate that it nests in forest vegetation, but details such as nest structure, clutch size, incubation, and care of young are not well established for the species as a whole. Breeding has been recorded in parts of Central America and Colombia, and Costa Rican observations indicate that reproduction occurs locally. More field study is needed to define its breeding season and nesting habits in Costa Rica.
value.dietFeeding: Its diet includes arthropods, small lizards, and fruit. It usually forages alone in the understory and midstory, perching quietly before making short sallies to glean prey from leaves or branches. It may sometimes hover briefly while taking food and occasionally joins mixed-species feeding flocks. Fruit is likely especially important when available in humid forest, but the relative importance of animal and plant foods varies by season and locality.
value.behavior: The Speckled Mourner is generally quiet and difficult to detect. It often sits motionless in shaded vegetation and moves through forest foliage with short, deliberate flights. Males give a repeated, ringing and somewhat ventriloquial song, while the species also produces a plaintive, drawn-out call. It may participate in mixed-species flocks, but it is more often encountered singly. Its preference for dense, wet forest and unobtrusive behavior contribute to its reputation as a scarce bird in Costa Rica.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing, although the species has a broad geographic range and is not currently judged to meet the thresholds for a threatened category.
